question: Who can join the DevLab Collective?
answer: Any student or recent graduate with basic programming experience can apply. You do not need to be an expert — curiosity, reliability and a willingness to receive code review matter most.

question: How do I apply?
answer: Use the contact form on the home page and choose “Join the Lab” as the subject. We open intake at the start of each semester and invite applicants to a short technical conversation and a small pairing exercise.

question: What is the weekly time commitment?
answer: Plan for about 6–8 hours a week: a planning or review session, a stand-up rhythm, and focused build time. Exam periods are planned around in advance.

question: Can I join remotely?
answer: Yes. Our workflow is built around Git, pull requests and async updates, so hybrid and remote members contribute fully. Demos and retrospectives run on video as well as in person.

question: How are projects chosen?
answer: Projects come from campus needs, community partners and open-source gaps. The mentors team scores each proposal on learning value, scope and user impact before it enters the roadmap.

question: Can I propose my own project?
answer: Absolutely. Submit a one-page proposal with the problem, target users and a rough tech stack. If approved, you become the product owner for the first sprint.

question: How do sprints work?
answer: Every sprint lasts two weeks: planning on day one, daily asynchronous stand-ups, a demo to stakeholders and a retrospective at the end. Velocity and bug counts are tracked on the project board.

question: Who owns the code we write?
answer: Lab projects are released under open-source licences chosen per project (usually MIT). Contributors keep credit for their commits and may reference the work in their portfolios.

question: Which languages and frameworks do you use?
answer: Mostly JavaScript/TypeScript (React, Node.js), Python (FastAPI) and SQL. We pick the right tool per project rather than forcing one stack, and mentors help you ramp up.

question: What does the CI/CD pipeline look like?
answer: Every pull request triggers linting, unit tests and a preview build. Merges to main run the full test suite, build container images and deploy to staging, with production releases gated by a reviewer.

question: What are the testing expectations?
answer: New features ship with tests. We aim for at least 80% coverage on business logic and require passing checks before a pull request can be merged.

question: Will the lab help with internships and jobs?
answer: Yes. Mentors from industry run mock interviews, review portfolios and share openings. Many members land internships after one or two semesters of lab work.

question: Do I get a certificate?
answer: Members who complete at least two sprints and one release receive a lab completion certificate and a written reference describing their contribution.

question: Is the lab free?
answer: Yes — membership is free. Hosting and tooling costs are covered by sponsors and university support.

question: How do I report a security issue in a lab project?
answer: Please email the lab address with “Security” in the subject and include steps to reproduce. We acknowledge reports promptly and credit responsible disclosure in our release notes.

question: How can industry partners get involved?
answer: Reach out through the contact form. Partners can sponsor projects, mentor teams, offer real-world problem statements or host demo days.
